workflows.title: Non-surgical retreatment — outcome assessment and procedure
workflows.overview:
## 1. Outcome assessment (minimum 1 year post-treatment)

Assess every root-filled tooth clinically and radiographically at least one year after treatment. Classify the outcome using ESE (2006) categories:

- **Favourable** — clinical and radiographic normality
- **Uncertain** — vague or irreproducible symptoms, mild discomfort; no change or reduction in lesion size radiographically
- **Unfavourable** — persistent apical periodontitis; radiolucency that is new, growing, or persistent after 4 years; or signs of external inflammatory root resorption

## 2. Branch by outcome

### Favourable
- No further action; routine recall.

### Uncertain
- Monitor with annual clinical and radiographic review for up to 4 years (exception: large lesions may need longer).
- If resolution is complete within 4 years → favourable; no further action.
- If still uncertain or worsening at 4 years → reclassify as unfavourable.

### Unfavourable
- Further treatment is indicated. Proceed to Stage 3.

## 3. Treatment decision for unfavourable outcome

For each unfavourable case, consider three options:

1. **Non-surgical retreatment** — ~80% prognosis at 2–4 years (Ng et al 2011a). Viable when:
   - Initial treatment was suboptimal (improvable)
   - Coronal seal failure is the cause
   - Patient is on IV bisphosphonates or antiangiogenic medications (extraction contraindicated)
   - Tooth needs a new coronal restoration (elective retreatment)

2. **Apical surgery** — preferred when retreatment has poor prognosis:
   - Initial treatment was of high standard (little room to improve)
   - High risk of procedural error: blocked or sclerosed canal, inaccessible perforation, large immovable post

3. **Extraction** — indicated when:
   - Gross tooth tissue loss
   - Periodontal disease
   - Unrestorable longitudinal tooth fracture
   - Extensive resorption
   - *Exception:* tooth with a large periapical lesion destined for implant may be retreated before extraction to allow alveolar bone regeneration

## 4. Pre-retreatment examination

Before proceeding, document:

### History specifics
- When was the tooth root filled?
- Where was treatment performed?
- How many visits?
- Was rubber dam used?
- When was the tooth last reviewed radiographically?

### Restorability gate
Confirm **≥2mm circumferential supragingival dentine** and **>30% original coronal volume** before committing. (Exception: space maintainer, overdenture abutment, or medical contraindication to extraction.)

### Radiographic assessment
- Root canal morphology
- Presence/absence of periradicular radiolucency
- Procedural errors: missed canals, transportation, ledges, perforations, separated instruments
- Obturation quality: extent, voids, filling material
- Coronal seal: subseal presence, restoration type, marginal integrity, caries

## 5. Re-establishment of access

### If coronal restoration is defective or core needs investigation
- Remove restoration using levering equipment or forceps cautiously — risk of tooth fracture
- Place temporary onlay/crown afterwards to allow dam placement and temporisation

### If crown is recently placed with sound margins
- Access through the restoration using diamond burs (porcelain) and tungsten carbide burs (metal)
- **Warn the patient before cutting through any ceramic restoration** — risk of cracks or fractures that affect aesthetics and function; document this discussion
- Teeth crowned to mask malposition or inclination should be referred

### Intra-pulpal core material
- Remove using ultrasonic tips or long-neck burs close to the pulpal floor/cavity walls
- Post cores or intraradicular cores → refer unless operator is experienced

## 6. Removal of intracanal obstructions

Intracanal obstructions (hard pastes, separated instruments, silver points, posts) are best managed under an **operating microscope**. Unless experienced, refer. Methods:

- Ultrasonic instruments to vibrate separated instruments free
- Specialised equipment for posts and silver points

## 7. Removal of obturation material

1. **Soften** with ultrasonic plasticisation of gutta-percha or solvents (Eucalyptol or Xylene) — solvents are toxic to periapical tissue; use with caution
2. **Bulk removal** with hand or NiTi rotary/reciprocating files in **crown-down** method; stainless steel hand files guide NiTi files
3. **Supplement with 17% EDTA** — dissolves sealers and inorganic dentine constituents, opens blockages
4. Do NOT use Gates-Glidden burs on hard obturation material — risk of instrument deflection and perforation
5. Take a confirmatory periapical radiograph after crown-down removal to check for residual gutta-percha tags; Hedstrom files + solvent for tags
6. Refer cases with flush/well-condensed obturations, over-extended obturation, silver points, or gutta-percha carriers unless experienced

## 8. Chemo-mechanical preparation, obturation, and restoration

Follow the same protocol as initial RCT:
- NiTi shaping + NaOCl irrigation (NaOCl effectiveness can be enhanced with automated agitation or manual master-cone agitation)
- Dry, obturate, restore using the same techniques and materials as initial treatment
- **Cuspal coverage restoration** is particularly important post-retreatment: incidence of cracks is higher in retreated teeth (Capar et al 2015); cuspal coverage provides a good coronal seal and resistance to fracture

## 9. Follow-up

Review clinically and radiographically at **≥1 year**. If healing is incomplete, review annually for up to **4 years**. Large lesions may take longer. If outcome remains unfavourable at 4 years, consider apical surgery or extraction.

workflows.title: Restoration of the root-canal-treated tooth
workflows.overview:
## 1. Restorability gate (assess BEFORE starting RCT)

Before committing to root canal treatment, confirm the tooth is restorable:

- **≥2mm circumferential supragingival dentine** present
- **>30% of original coronal tooth volume** remaining (Al-Nuaimi et al 2017, 2020)

Favourable outcomes are significantly higher above the 30% threshold; outcomes below it are significantly worse. If these thresholds are not met, reconsider tooth retention.

The two key survival predictors are: (1) quantity of sound residual tooth structure (Al-Nuaimi et al 2020) and (2) choice of restoration (Pratt 2016). The most common reason root-filled teeth are extracted is restorative failure, not biological failure (Fuss et al 1999).

## 2. Ferrule decision

For any indirect restoration, provide an optimum **ferrule**:

- **Height:** 1.5–2.5mm of supragingival dentine (Juloski et al 2012)
- **Thickness:** minimum 2mm (Nagasiri and Chitmongkolsuk 2005)
- The ferrule allows the extra-coronal restoration margin to sit on sound tooth tissue without encroaching on the biological width
- If adequate ferrule height cannot be achieved, consider crown lengthening or orthodontic extrusion before proceeding

## 3. Cuspal coverage decision

Assess how many proximal walls remain:

### Class I (no proximal wall loss)
- Cuspal coverage **not required** if all remaining walls have adequate thickness and no cracks are present

### One proximal wall missing (posterior tooth)
- Cuspal coverage restoration is **required** in most cases

### Two or more walls missing
- Cuspal coverage is **almost always** required. In this situation, reverse the burden of proof — try to justify why cuspal coverage should NOT be used; circumstances where it can be avoided will be rare

The garden-shed analogy: the structural integrity of a shed depends on all walls and the roof being present and fixed together. Loss of any wall significantly undermines the structure — the tooth behaves the same way under occlusal load.

Cuspal coverage protects by: eliminating exposed tooth/restoration interfaces vulnerable to point loading; spreading load across the whole occlusal surface; preventing flexion and fracture of residual tooth structure.

## 4. Post decision

A post is only indicated when there is insufficient coronal tooth structure to retain a core by other means.

- **Purpose:** retain the core only — a post does NOT strengthen the root and does NOT substitute for the ferrule (Mannocci et al 2021)
- **Material:** choice of post material has no effect on tooth survival
- **Dentine sacrifice:** advances in adhesive technology mean there is no need to sacrifice further dentine to place a post; posts should remain passive in the canal
- **Length:** ideally longer than the clinical crown height; a **minimum of 4–5mm of root filling must be left apically** to preserve the apical seal (Figure 8.3)

## 5. Restoration type

For premolars and molars where cuspal coverage is indicated:

- Metal, metal-ceramic, all-ceramic, and indirect composite onlays/crowns all show excellent outcomes
- Direct cuspal coverage with composite resin is an option — provides an immediate definitive restoration with minimal further tooth tissue loss

## 6. Terminal and lone-standing teeth

Teeth with only one proximal contact, no proximal contacts, or the terminal molar are at increased structural risk. Pay attention to:

- Excessive occlusal forces
- Premature occlusal interferences
- Dynamic loading in excursive and protrusive guidance

firstPrinciples.title: Apical periodontitis is caused by infection of the root canal system
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Understanding what drives periapical disease determines the entire logic of root canal treatment.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The biological basis of root canal treatment

Apical periodontitis does not arise from the pulp dying alone — it arises because a dead pulp creates a warm, moist, nutrient-rich environment that allows oral bacteria to colonise the canal space [1]. Once infected, microorganisms organise as planktonic (fluid-phase) bacteria or as dense biofilm communities adhering to the canal walls [2]. The goal of treatment is therefore dual: eliminate microorganisms from the canal system, and prevent reinfection with a well-sealed root canal filling and coronal restoration [3].

## Clinical application

This principle explains why both chemo-mechanical preparation AND an adequate coronal seal are non-negotiable. Addressing one without the other leaves a pathway for failure.

citations.quote: Pulp death and subsequent necrosis renders the root canal space undefended and provides an ideal warm and moist environment with an abundant nutrient source to support microbial proliferation.

Primary endodontic infections are caused by oral bacteria which are usually opportunistic pathogens. Once the root canal space is infected, endodontic microbiota exist in a fluid phase or, as dense bacterial aggregates/coaggregates adhering to the root canal walls forming multi-layered communities that resemble biofilm.
Treatment is aimed at eliminating microorganisms from the root canal system and preventing reinfection with a well-sealed root canal filling and coronal restoration.

firstPrinciples.title: Four factors predict primary RCT success
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: These four variables are the strongest modifiable and non-modifiable determinants of primary RCT outcome identified in the literature.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The four predictors

Four factors have been shown to significantly improve the outcome of primary root canal treatment [1]:

- Pre-operative absence of periapical radiolucency
- Root filling with no voids
- Root filling extending within 2mm of the radiographic apex
- Satisfactory coronal seal and restoration

## Clinical application

The operator cannot change the pre-operative periapical status — but they must note it and communicate its prognostic impact to the patient. The other three predictors are entirely within the operator's control: void-free obturation, correct length, and a definitive coronal seal placed without delay.

citations.quote: Four factors have been shown to significantly improve the outcome of primary root canal treatment: Pre-operative absence of periapical radiolucency; Root filling with no voids; Root filling extending within 2mm of the radiographic apex; Satisfactory coronal seal and restoration.

firstPrinciples.title: Mechanical preparation cannot reach the entire root canal system
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: This anatomical reality shifts the burden of disinfection from files to chemical irrigants.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The anatomical limit of instruments

No instrument can contact every surface of the root canal system — lateral canals, fins, and anastomoses remain uninstrumented regardless of technique [1]. The biological objectives of treatment (disinfecting as much of the system as possible, removing nutrient sources, and preventing recontamination) therefore rely on chemical irrigants to reach areas files cannot [2].

## Clinical application

This is why irrigation is not a supplementary step — it is the primary disinfection mechanism. Irrigation is also the only way to impact those areas of the root canal wall not touched by mechanical instrumentation [3].

citations.quote: It is not possible to mechanically prepare the entire root canal system; the operator is therefore reliant on other methods of cleaning to achieve the following biological objectives.

To disinfect as much of the root canal system as possible; To remove any potential nutrient source that will sustain or promote proliferation of microorganisms in the root canal system; To prevent recontamination of the root canal system.
Irrigation is also the only way to impact those areas of the root canal wall not touched by mechanical instrumentation.

firstPrinciples.title: Rubber dam is mandatory; inability to apply it is a restorability signal
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Rubber dam isolation is both an infection-control requirement and a diagnostic check on restorability.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why rubber dam is mandatory

The dam serves four functions: minimising contamination of the canal by oral bacteria, preventing ingestion or aspiration of materials and instruments, providing a controlled operative environment, and improving visualisation [1].

## The restorability signal

If rubber dam cannot be applied technically, this is not just an inconvenience — it triggers a reassessment. The source states directly: if it is not technically possible to apply the dam, then restorability of the tooth and the reason for carrying out root canal treatment must be challenged [2]. A tooth that cannot be isolated may not be sufficiently intact to justify treatment.

citations.quote: A rubber dam is used to: Minimise the risk of contamination of the root canal system by oral bacteria in saliva and other tissue fluids; Prevent ingestion or aspiration of dental materials, irrigants and instruments; Provide a controlled operative environment; Improve visualisation of the operating field.

The use of a rubber dam is mandatory for root canal treatment. If it is not technically possible to apply the dam then restorability of the tooth and the reason for carrying root canal treatment must be challenged.

firstPrinciples.title: Crown-down NiTi shaping offers three mechanical advantages over step-back
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The sequence in which the canal is widened — coronal first or apical first — has measurable consequences for debris, instrument stress, and irrigant delivery.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The crown-down rationale

The crown-down approach — widening the canal from coronal to apical — is widely accepted as the preferred method for three explicit reasons [1]:

1. Bulk removal of infected material early in the preparation sequence
2. Reduced stress on subsequent instruments used deeper in the canal
3. Better irrigant exchange throughout the canal

## Clinical application

Step-back (apical-first) techniques deliver the thinnest, most stress-susceptible instruments to the most curved apical region before any coronal dentine has been removed. Crown-down reverses this: by the time apical files are used, the coronal canal is already widened, providing straight-line access and reducing cyclic fatigue on the apical instruments.

citations.quote: This crown-down approach allows for bulk removal of infected material early in the preparation. It will reduce stress on subsequent instruments used deeper in the canal and facilitate better irrigant exchange.

firstPrinciples.title: NiTi files are for enlargement only; the glidepath must precede them
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: NiTi rotary files are optimised for shaping, not navigation — using them to negotiate unprepared canals is a primary cause of instrument separation.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The principle

The source is explicit: NiTi files are for canal enlargement and not negotiation; a glidepath should have been established prior to file insertion [1]. Initial negotiation must be made with a stainless steel hand instrument — this is true even when engine-driven NiTi glidepath files are used.

## Clinical application

The glidepath is a smooth, unimpeded pathway from the orifice to the anatomical foramen [2]. Without it, a NiTi file engaging an uncurved, uninstrumented canal has no path to follow — it locks, stresses, and separates. Small stainless steel files (sizes 6, 8, 10) in a watch-winding motion create this path before any powered instrument enters.

citations.quote: NiTi files are for canal enlargement and not negotiation; A glidepath should have been established prior to file insertion.
The glidepath is a smooth unimpeded pathway or 'approach' from the coronal orifice of the canal to its terminus at the anatomical foramen to allow larger instruments to follow.

firstPrinciples.title: Patency files must not exceed size 10 or extend more than 1mm beyond the foramen
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Maintaining canal patency is beneficial, but the technique has narrow safety margins that, if breached, cause the very complications it aims to prevent.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What patency achieves

Passing a small file through the apical foramen reduces debris and soft tissue accumulation in the apical portion, decreases procedural error risk, and may mechanically dislodge bacteria at the foramen [1].

## The safety limit

Only small instruments (sizes 6, 8, or 10) should be used, and they must not extend greater than 1mm beyond the confines of the canal [2]. Exceeding this limit causes over-instrumentation, enlargement or transportation of the foramen, extrusion of infected debris, and mechanical trauma to the apical tissues [3].

citations.quote: Using a patency technique is thought to reduce the risk of accumulation of debris and soft tissue in the apical portion of the canal and therefore decreases the risk of procedural error. It is also suggested that the mechanical action of a patency file may help remove bacteria that are present in the apical constriction and foramen.
When using a patency technique it must be emphasised that only small instruments should be used and they should not be extended greater than 1mm beyond the confines of the canal.
Violation of this principle can lead to over-instrumentation, enlargement or transportation of the foramen, extrusion of infected debris and mechanical trauma to the apical tissues.

firstPrinciples.title: NaOCl 0.5–5.25% is the irrigant of choice; 0.2% CHX mouthwash is not acceptable
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Irrigant selection and concentration are not interchangeable — effectiveness and safety depend on using the right agents at the right strengths.
firstPrinciples.body:
## NaOCl as primary irrigant

A stabilised sodium hypochlorite solution at 0.5% to 5.25% is the recommended antibacterial irrigant [1]. Its advantages are: antimicrobial action, tissue-dissolving capability, and reduction of friction between instruments and dentine. It is the only way to reach canal walls untouched by mechanical instruments.

## EDTA and CHX roles

17% EDTA is a chelating agent used to remove the smear layer from dentine [2]. 2% chlorhexidine has a wide range of antimicrobial activity and the property of substantivity — retaining effectiveness for an extended period after application [3].

## The concentration prohibition

0.2% chlorhexidine — the concentration sold as mouthwash — is explicitly not considered an appropriate antibacterial agent for endodontic use [4]. The clinical-grade concentration required is 2%.

citations.quote: An active antibacterial agent should be used such as a stabilised sodium hypochlorite solution at a concentration of 0.5% to 5.25%.
EDTA is a chelating agent and used to remove the smear layer.

Chlorhexidine is a cationic solution which has a wide range of antimicrobial activity and unique feature called substantivity, which is the ability of an antimicrobial agent to retain its effectiveness for an extended period.
Note: 0.2% Chlorhexidine which is sold as mouthwash is not considered an appropriate antibacterial agent for endodontic use.

firstPrinciples.title: Five precautions reduce hypochlorite extrusion risk
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: NaOCl is caustic — extrusion into periapical tissues causes a serious hypochlorite accident. The technique of delivery determines risk.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The hazard

NaOCl extrusion causes a hypochlorite accident — a serious adverse event. The risk is increased when irrigation technique is careless.

## The five technical precautions

The source lists five specific measures to reduce this risk [1]:

1. Use a **side-venting needle** (prevents direct apical jet)
2. Apply **finger** pressure — not thumb pressure (gives finer control)
3. **Never lock** the needle in the canal
4. **Do not advance** the needle to full working length
5. **Pre-operatively identify** open apices or perforations (these create pathways for extrusion)

## Clinical application

All five precautions address the mechanism of accidental extrusion: high pressure in a locked system with an open exit. The precautions prevent each component of that mechanism.

citations.quote: The risk can be reduced by using a side venting needle, using a finger rather than thumb pressure, never locking the needle in the canal, not advancing the needle to full working length and careful pre-operative assessment to identify open apicies or perforations.

firstPrinciples.title: Retreatment prognosis is approximately 80% at 2–4 years
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Knowing the retreatment prognosis quantitatively allows the clinician to present a specific evidence-based figure when discussing treatment options.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The evidence base

The prognosis of non-surgical retreatment, assessed two to four years after treatment, is estimated to be 80% (Ng et al 2011a) [1]. This is a prospective evidence-based figure, not an estimate from clinical impression.

## Clinical application

This figure makes retreatment a viable option when extraction is contraindicated — for example in patients on IV bisphosphonates or antiangiogenic medications [2]. It also supports elective retreatment before placing a new coronal restoration on a tooth with a suboptimal root filling. The figure is not a ceiling — it is the starting prognosis for cases selected appropriately.

citations.quote: The prognosis of retreatment, after two to four years following treatment, is estimated to be 80% (Ng et al 2011a).
Therefore it may be a viable treatment option if the tooth is to be retained or where its removal is contraindicated e.g. patients on IV bisphosphonates or antiangiogenic medications.

firstPrinciples.title: Cracks are more common in retreated teeth, making cuspal coverage especially important
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The retreatment process itself increases crack risk — this biomechanical consequence changes the restoration decision.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The evidence

The incidence of cracks is higher in teeth undergoing retreatment (Capar et al 2015) [1]. The source attributes this to the combined effect of the original preparation, the retreatment procedure (including solvent application, ultrasonic use, and repeated instrumentation), and post-space preparation if relevant.

## Clinical application

Because retreated teeth are at elevated crack risk, cuspal coverage restorations are particularly important in this group. They provide a good coronal seal and resistance to fracture, improving long-term prognosis [2].

citations.quote: Care should also be observed during the obturation phase as the incidence of cracks is higher in teeth undergoing retreatment (Capar et al 2015).
Cuspal coverage restorations capable of providing a good coronal seal and resistance to fracture are important for the long-term prognosis of retreated teeth (Ng et al a, b).

firstPrinciples.title: The most common reason root-filled teeth are extracted is restorative failure, not biological failure
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: This reverses the common assumption that endodontic technique alone determines the fate of root-filled teeth.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The finding

Most research on post-treatment failure focuses on biological failure and re-emergence of endodontic disease. However, the most common reason for root-filled teeth being extracted is restorative complications (Fuss et al 1999) — structural failure, not biological failure [1].

## Clinical application

This means that planning the definitive restoration is as important as the endodontic technique itself. Survival studies confirm that the main factors influencing survival are the quantity of sound residual tooth structure (Al-Nuaimi et al 2020) and the choice of restoration (Pratt 2016) [2]. Assessing and planning the restoration before starting RCT is therefore not optional.

citations.quote: The most common reason for root filled teeth to be extracted is because of restorative complications (Fuss et al 1999) which relate to structural failure.

Survival studies have shown that the main factors influencing the survival of root filled teeth are: the quantity of sound residual tooth structure (Al-Nuaimi et al 2020) and the choice of restoration (Pratt 2016).

firstPrinciples.title: Ferrule requires 1.5–2.5mm height and 2mm minimum thickness
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The ferrule effect has been defined dimensionally in the literature — knowing the threshold allows the clinician to determine whether a predictable indirect restoration is feasible.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The dimensional thresholds

A review by Juloski et al (2012) established a minimum ferrule height of 1.5–2.5mm [1]. Nagasiri and Chitmongkolsuk (2005) defined a minimum thickness of 2mm [2]. The ferrule allows the margins of an extra-coronal restoration to sit on sound tooth tissue around the entire circumference, preventing microleakage and resisting dislodgement forces.

## Clinical application

If these dimensions cannot be achieved with the existing tooth structure, the clinician must either modify the plan (crown lengthening, orthodontic extrusion) or reconsider the restoration type. A post does not substitute for insufficient ferrule — the two serve different structural roles.

citations.quote: A review by Juloski et al (2012) suggested a minimum ferrule height of 1.5–2.5mm is required with a minimum thickness of 2mm (Nagasiri and Chitmongkolsuk 2005).
Therefore clinicians should make every effort to provide an optimum ferrule when planning indirect restorations (Mannocci et al 2021).

firstPrinciples.title: 30% remaining tooth volume is the critical threshold for predictable RCT outcome
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Quantifying residual tooth volume as a percentage gives a measurable, objective restorability criterion.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The threshold

Early research using intra-oral scanners and CAD/CAM technology found that a remaining tooth volume of 30% is a critical threshold. Favourable outcomes of root-treated teeth were significantly higher when more than 30% of the original tooth structure was present; the converse applied when less than 30% remained (Al-Nuaimi et al 2017 and 2020) [1].

## Clinical application

This 30% figure gives the clinician an objective benchmark for the restorability gate. It supplements the minimum 2mm circumferential dentine criterion. Below this threshold, committing to RCT without a clear plan for the structural deficit is not justifiable.

citations.quote: Early research has suggested that a remaining tooth volume of 30% is a critical threshold in terms of the predictability of a favourable or unfavourable outcome. Favourable outcomes of root treated teeth were significantly higher when more than 30% of the original tooth tissue structure was present. The converse applied if there was less than 30% (Al-Nuaimi et al 2017 and Al-Nuaimi et al 2020).

firstPrinciples.title: A post retains the core only; it does not strengthen the root or substitute for a ferrule
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The purpose of an intracanal post is widely misunderstood — this principle corrects the three commonest misconceptions.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What a post does and does not do

The source is unambiguous: the purpose of the post is to retain the core. It is not to strengthen the root or compensate for the absence of the ferrule effect (Mannocci et al 2021) [1].

## Practical corollaries

Because adhesive technology has advanced, there is no need to sacrifice further dentine to place a post — posts should remain passive in the canal space [2]. The choice of post material has no effect on tooth survival [3]. These facts together mean a post should only be placed when the tooth genuinely cannot retain a core without one.

citations.quote: The purpose of the post is to retain the core. It is not to strengthen the root or compensate for the absence of the ferrule effect (Mannocci et al 2021).
With advances in adhesive technology there is no need to sacrifice further dentine to facilitate a post's placement. Posts should remain passive in the root canal space.
The choice of post material has no effect on the survival of the tooth.

firstPrinciples.title: Post length must exceed crown height; a minimum of 4–5mm GP must remain apically
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Post length is constrained at both ends — retention above and apical seal below — and these constraints define the safe range.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The dual constraint

Post length should ideally be longer than the clinical crown it is restoring — this ensures the post provides adequate retention for the core. At the same time, a minimum of 4–5mm of root filling material must be left in the apical portion so as not to disturb the apical seal [1].

## Clinical application

The two constraints set a working range. If the available canal length between orifice and the 4–5mm apical limit is not long enough to exceed the crown height, a post may not be feasible, or the tooth may not be suitable for a post-retained crown. In such cases, the restoration plan must be revised.

citations.quote: Post length should ideally be longer that the clinical crown it is restoring - but a minimum of 4-5mm of root filling material should be left so it does not disturb the apical seal.
